notes.meaning: God tells Moses to cut out two new stone tablets like the first set he broke. The Lord promised to write the very same words on them. This showed that God was willing to renew his covenant, his sacred agreement, with Israel after their sin with the golden calf. Having Moses cut the stones himself was a gentle reminder of the damage their sin had caused.

Moses is instructed to be ready the next morning and climb Mount Sinai alone. He is to present himself before God at the top of the mountain. God did not cancel Moses' special task, but invited him into another quiet morning meeting in his presence.

No other person or grazing animal was permitted anywhere near Mount Sinai while God met with Moses. This strict boundary reminded the people of the awesome holiness of God and showed that sinful people must approach him with reverence. Moses stood alone as the go-between for the entire nation.

Moses obeyed God promptly by shaping two stone tablets and climbing Mount Sinai early in the morning. The stone slabs were light enough for him to carry both in his hands. His quick obedience showed his eager desire to meet with the Lord and receive his instructions.

The Lord came down in a cloud and stood there with Moses on the mountaintop. God then proclaimed his holy name, the Lord. The cloud veiled the full brilliance of God's majesty from human eyes while clearly showing his real presence.

The Lord passed before Moses and announced his true nature and character. He declared that he is full of tender compassion, gracious to the undeserving, patient with sinners, and rich in faithful love and truth. Here God reveals that at his very core, he delights in showing mercy.

God explains that his faithful love extends to thousands of generations, forgiving all kinds of wrongdoing. At the same time, his holy justice will never overlook obstinate sin, and its destructive effects continue down through families that reject him. God's mercy is vastly greater than his wrath, but he never compromises his justice.

other.label: Catholic
other.view: The Latin Vulgate translation underlying the Douay-Rheims translates the middle clause to say that no person is innocent of themselves before God.

other.label: Popular modern teaching
other.view: Some modern deliverance ministries teach that this verse describes inherited spiritual curses that pass down to Christians and must be broken through special rituals.

notes.meaning: As soon as Moses heard the Lord proclaim his name, he dropped to the ground in worship. Hearing of God's great mercy and holiness filled him with deep awe and gratitude. Learning who God really is always leads the heart into humble adoration.

Moses pleads with God to stay with the people on their journey, forgive their rebellion, and keep them as his special possession. He freely confesses that Israel is stubborn, using their desperate weakness as a reason to ask for God's presence. Moses knew they could never reach the promised land without God's ongoing grace.

God answers Moses by renewing his covenant with the people. He promises to perform astonishing miracles before the whole nation, wonders never before seen anywhere on the earth. These powerful acts would prove to everyone that Israel belonged to the living God.

The Lord tells the people to carefully obey everything he commands them. In return, he promises to drive out the six warlike nations living in the land of Canaan. Israel could never conquer the land by their own power; the victory would be entirely God's work.

Israel is strongly warned never to make a treaty with the pagan peoples living in Canaan. Making friends with idol worshippers would soon become a dangerous trap that would pull them away from God. Compromising with spiritual danger always leads to ruin.

The Israelites are commanded to completely destroy the local false religion. They had to tear down the pagan altars, smash the stone pillars, and chop down the wooden poles used to worship the goddess Asherah. God wanted no pagan monuments left behind to tempt his people back into idolatry.

God forbids Israel from bowing down to any other god. He explains that his very name is Jealous, meaning he cares passionately for the total devotion of his people. Just as a faithful spouse guards the marriage bond, God will not share his worship with worthless idols.

Israel must refuse treaties with the Canaanites because friendly contact would lead to sharing in their sacrificial feasts. If Israelite men married pagan daughters, those wives would persuade them to worship false gods. Close alliances with unbelievers quickly lead God's people into serious spiritual unfaithfulness.

God commands the people never to cast metal idols for themselves. This rule struck directly at their recent sin with the golden calf. No physical statue made by human hands can ever represent the living God or receive the worship that belongs to him alone.

The people are told to celebrate the Feast of Unleavened Bread for seven days in the month of Abib. Eating bread baked without yeast served as a yearly reminder of how quickly God had rescued them from Egypt. Keeping this festival helped them remember their deliverance with thankful hearts.

Every firstborn male belongs to God, whether from livestock or human families. An unclean animal like a donkey had to be bought back with a sacrificial lamb or put to death, and every firstborn son had to be redeemed by a payment. Giving back the firstborn acknowledged that God owns everything and that he had spared Israel's firstborn sons in Egypt.

God commands his people to work for six days and rest on the seventh day. This weekly rest had to be kept even during the busy seasons of plowing and harvesting. Trusting God means putting regular worship and rest ahead of our pressing work deadlines.

Israel is told to keep two other annual harvest festivals: the Feast of Weeks for the early wheat harvest and the Feast of Ingathering at the end of the agricultural year. These gatherings gave the nation set times to dedicate their first crops to God. Joyful thankfulness was built right into the rhythm of their yearly life.

All the men of Israel were required to travel three times each year to appear before the Lord God. Gathering at the central place of worship showed their ongoing loyalty to the God who had chosen them. Coming together regularly strengthened their faith and their unity as one people.

God promises to clear out enemy nations and expand Israel's territory. He also promises that no enemy will even try to take their land while the men are away at the three annual feasts. God showed that when his people put worship first, he personally guards their homes and families.

God forbids offering the blood of his sacrifices with leavened bread, and commands that none of the Passover meat be left over until morning. Leaving out yeast was a picture of moral purity, while finishing the meal showed respect for a sacred feast. Worship must always be kept free from corruption and careless neglect.

The people were to bring the finest of their early crops to the house of the Lord their God. In addition, they were forbidden from cooking a young goat in its mother's milk, which was likely a superstitious pagan custom. Honoring God means offering him our very best while turning away from ungodly traditions.

The Lord commands Moses to write down these covenant terms as an enduring written record. God was officially re-establishing his sacred bond with Israel through Moses as their mediator. Putting the commands in writing ensured that future generations would know God's will accurately.

Moses stayed on the mountain with the Lord for forty days and forty nights without eating any food or drinking water. God miraculously sustained his physical life while they were in close communion. The Lord wrote the fundamental terms of the covenant, the Ten Commandments, onto the two stone tablets.

When Moses walked down Mount Sinai with the two tablets in his hands, his face was shining brightly because he had been speaking with God. Moses was not even aware that his face was glowing. Spending intimate time in the Lord's presence leaves the beauty of his holiness resting on his servants.

other.label: Catholic
other.view: The Latin Vulgate translated the description of Moses' radiant face with a Latin word meaning 'horned,' which led traditional Catholic artwork and older Bibles like the Douay-Rheims to portray Moses with physical horns.

other.label: Modern scholarship
other.view: Scholars note that the Hebrew term comes from the word for horn used in the sense of shooting out rays of light, meaning bright beams radiated from the skin of his face.

notes.meaning: Aaron and all the Israelites saw the radiant light beaming from Moses' face and were terrified to approach him. Their fear was fueled by their guilty consciences after their recent rebellion, as well as the sheer majesty of God's reflected glory. True holiness inspires deep awe, and an awareness of personal sin makes people pull back.

Moses called out to them, so Aaron and the leaders found courage to return, followed by the rest of the nation. Moses then passed on every commandment the Lord had spoken to him on the mountaintop. The radiant glow on Moses' face confirmed to everyone that his message was truly from heaven.

When Moses finished giving the Lord's commands to the people, he covered his face with a veil. He veiled himself so the overwhelming brightness would not keep the people from approaching him in daily life. The veil also illustrated how the deeper spiritual truths of the Old Testament were partially hidden until Christ came.

Whenever Moses entered the Lord's presence in the tabernacle, he took off the veil until he came back out. Then he delivered God's words to the people with an open face. Nothing can be hidden from God, so believers can come before him with complete openness and honesty.

The people would look at Moses and see his face shining each time he returned from speaking with God. Moses would then put the veil back over his face until his next conversation with the Lord. This ongoing cycle showed that true spiritual brightness comes from continually drawing near to God.
